Networks are classified by the area they cover. A personal area network links a person's own devices over a few metres, often by Bluetooth. A local area network covers one site and is owned and managed by the organisation.

A metropolitan area network covers a town or city, linking sites such as council buildings or university campuses. A wide area network spans countries, using telecommunications links leased from third parties; the internet is the largest WAN.

A topology is the arrangement of devices and links. A bus shares one backbone cable, so it is cheap but suffers collisions and fails if the backbone breaks. A ring passes data around a loop in one direction with no collisions, but one break can stop it.

A star connects each device to a central switch, isolating cable faults and giving high performance, though the switch is a single point of failure. A mesh gives multiple routes, providing resilience at high cost.

A network interface card provides the physical connection and a unique MAC address. A switch forwards frames within a LAN to the correct port using MAC addresses. A router joins different networks and forwards packets between them using IP addresses and routing tables.

Local area network (LAN)?
A network covering a single site or building, with infrastructure owned and managed by the organisation.
Wide area network (WAN)?
A network covering a large geographical area, connecting LANs using third-party telecommunications links.
Topology?
The physical or logical arrangement of the devices and links in a network.
Switch?
A device that connects devices within a LAN and forwards each frame only to the port of its destination, using MAC addresses.
Router?
A device that connects different networks and forwards packets towards their destination using IP addresses and routing tables.
Gateway?
A device that connects two networks using different protocols and translates between them.

Many questions ask you to recommend and justify a topology or device for a scenario. A justification needs a feature and its benefit in context, for example 'a star topology means a cable fault in one guest room only affects that room, so the rest of the hotel stays online'. When comparing, use the same criteria for each option (reliability, performance, cost, scalability). Do not describe a switch as broadcasting data, that is a hub, and remember routers use IP addresses while switches use MAC addresses.
